title: A Biography of Earth
intro: Earth's life story in four chapters (eons): Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic, Phanerozoic. For each one, learn WHAT happened and WHY it mattered.

sections.title: Hadean Eon: the molten start
bullets: Hadean = **4.57 to 3.8 Ga**. It starts when Earth forms by **planetesimal accretion** (small rocks crashing together and sticking).
Three heat sources: **gravitational collapse**, **impacts**, **radioactive decay**. Hot enough to partly melt by ~4.5 Ga.
**Chemical differentiation**: molten iron sinks to the centre (core); the **ultramafic mantle** stays as a thick outer shell.
Slide 4 (artist's picture): a glowing, lava-covered surface with a giant impact explosion. It shows the Hadean ingredients: a partly molten surface, volcanoes and asteroid impacts (Textbook 8.3).

Slide 5 (artist's picture, no caption): steaming volcanic vents beside a young sea. Textbook 8.3: minerals dated 4.4 Ga show liquid water already existed. Water may come from volcanic outgassing, comets and meteorites, possibly all three (Textbook 8.3.3).

Slide 6 is the **time scale column**: Hadean at the bottom (birth of Earth 4,570 Ma), then Archean, Proterozoic, Phanerozoic on top. The Phanerozoic splits into Paleozoic (to 251 Ma), Mesozoic (to 65 Ma), Cenozoic (to 0). The arrow marks **Precambrian** = Hadean + Archean + Proterozoic = everything before 542 Ma.
The key on slide 6: **Ka** = thousand years ago, **Ma** = million years ago, **Ga** = billion years ago.

boxes.text: Why did iron sink? Iron is much denser than rock. While Earth was molten, gravity sorted it like oil and vinegar in a jar: heavy at the bottom, light on top. That is why Earth has layers today.
Hadean sounds like Hades, the underworld: hot, molten, hellish.
Dates differ by source. Your slide says the Hadean runs 4.57 to 3.8 Ga. The textbook says 4.5 to 4.0 Ga. Use the slide's numbers on the exam.

Slide 6 shows the Mesozoic ending at 65 Ma, but slide 49 and the textbook say 66 Ma. Paleozoic end: slide 251 Ma, textbook 252 Ma. Phanerozoic start: slide 542 Ma, textbook 541 Ma. Use the slide numbers and expect small differences.

sections.title: Building the first continents: arcs and greenstone belts
bullets: Slide 7 is a **cross-section (not to scale)** of an early ocean. Labelled: a **rift filled with volcanic rocks** (B), **volcanic arcs** (C and E), an **oceanic plateau** (D) above a rising magma plume, plus magma, sediment, oceanic crust and lithospheric mantle.
The legend says **hot-spot igneous rock** will become **greenstone** and **arc rock** will become **granite/gneiss**.
An **island arc** is a chain of volcanoes made when an oceanic plate sinks under another oceanic plate. Several arcs can combine and eventually evolve into a continent (Textbook 8.4.2).

Slide 9 shows the next step: the arcs, plateau and rift pieces (A to E) are squeezed together into one block. The slice of dark volcanic rock between them is the **greenstone belt**. Below it, **remelted crust** (red) and a **gneissic fabric** mark where the block is cooked and remelted. Asthenosphere sits on both sides.
**Greenstone** is metamorphosed basalt that gets its green colour from the mineral chlorite (Textbook 6, metamorphic rocks).

Slide 8 is only a title: 'Google Earth Caribbean plate'. The prof showed the Caribbean plate live. It is presumably a modern place with island arcs, but the slide gives no text, so ask or check your lecture notes.

boxes.text: Why is making the first continents a puzzle? Plate tectonics needs continents, but the easiest way to make continental rock is to melt existing continents (chicken and egg, Textbook 8.4.2). The slides answer with arcs: sinking oceanic plates feed volcanic arcs, and arcs and plateaus pile up and fuse into a larger, lighter, more felsic block.
Think of LEGO. Arcs, plateaus and rifts are the bricks, subduction is the hand that keeps pressing them together, and the greenstone belt is the seam between bricks.

Do not swap the two rock types on slide 7: hot-spot/ocean rock becomes GREENSTONE; arc rock becomes GRANITE/GNEISS. Also, slide 62 asks how continental crust was extracted from the mantle: the answer supported by slides 7 and 9 is subduction zones (arcs), not hot spots or ridges.

sections.title: Archean Eon: first rocks, first life
bullets: Slide 10 graph: continents grew fastest in the Archean. About **80%** of today's continental area existed by the end of it (~2.5 Ga).
Slides 12-14: **stromatolites**, layered mounds built by microbial mats (photosynthesising bacteria). Slide 11 shows microfossils (10 µm wide).
Textbook: first well-preserved fossils are stromatolites ~3.5 Ga.

Slide 10 curve shape: it starts near 0% at about 3.8 Ga, climbs steeply, reaches about 80% at 2.5 Ga, then flattens toward 100% through the Proterozoic and Phanerozoic. So the continents were mostly built early and then only slowly added to.

boxes.text: Why do stromatolites have layers? Textbook 8.4.3: they are fossils of photosynthetic microbial mats, so each layer is one mat of microbes stacked on the last. (Layer-by-layer growth detail: outside source, general knowledge.)
Slide 10 shows the continents mostly formed in the Archean, so an exam question asking 'when was most continental crust extracted from the mantle?' wants Archean, not Phanerozoic.

sections.title: Cratons and the assembly of North America
bullets: Slide 15: **protero** = first, **zoic** = life. The name came before Archean life was discovered.

Slide 16 is a world map of **geologic provinces**. Legend: stretched crust, large igneous provinces, Phanerozoic orogens, Phanerozoic basins, Phanerozoic platforms, **Precambrian shields**, and Archean crustal remnants. Each continent has an old core of shields and platforms ringed by younger belts.

A **craton** is the stable interior of a continent, mostly formed in the Archean. It has a **shield** (crystalline basement rock at the surface) and a **platform** (sedimentary rock covering the shield) (Textbook 8.4.2).

Slide 17 (North America): the **Shield** (orange) is in Canada; the **Western platform** and **Eastern platform** lie to its south, with Paleozoic and Mesozoic cover. Around the craton are the Phanerozoic orogens (Cordillera and Rocky Mountains in the west, Appalachians in the east, Ouachitas in the south) and the Coastal Plain.

Slide 18 is the 'assembly of North America'. Grey **Archean provinces (>2.5 Ga)** (Superior, Slave, Rae and Hearn, Wyoming) form the core. Younger belts wrap around: Proterozoic accreted crust (2.0 to 1.8 Ga), Trans-Hudson and other collisional orogens (1.9 to 1.8 Ga), **Yavapai** (1.8 to 1.7 Ga), **Mazatzal** (1.7 to 1.6 Ga), granite-rhyolite (1.5 to 1.3 Ga) and the **Grenville orogen** (1.3 to 1.0 Ga) on the east and south. Pink = younger, post-Precambrian crust outside the craton edge.

boxes.text: Why do cratons survive? Most tectonic activity happens around cratons rather than within them (Textbook 8.4.2), so their ancient rock stays almost unchanged.
A continent grows like tree rings, oldest in the middle: Archean core, then 2.0 to 1.8 Ga belts, then Yavapai, Mazatzal, and finally Grenville at the edge.

Shield and platform are different parts of the same craton. Shield = exposed crystalline rock; platform = sedimentary layers on top. Also, although slide 18 sits in the Proterozoic part of the deck, the grey core is Archean.

sections.title: Proterozoic Eon: oxygen and big continents
bullets: **protero** = first, **zoic** = life. It was named before Archean life was discovered (slide 15).
**Banded iron formations (BIFs)** are the evidence of oxygen build-up (slide 21).
Supercontinents: **Rodinia** (~750 Ma, slide 19) and **Pannotia** (formed ~600 Ma, short-lived, slide 20).
Last 500 Ma: **Ediacara fauna**, soft-bodied multicellular animals like worms and jellyfish (slides 22-23).
Slide 25: strata with large clasts in mudstone show glaciers (ice carries any size of rock).

boxes.text: Why do BIFs show oxygen? Before oxygen, iron dissolved in seawater. When cyanobacteria released O2, the iron rusted out of the water as iron oxide and settled in layers. No oxygen = no rust layers. Today's steel comes from this iron.
BIF = 'Big Iron Fingerprint' of the ocean's first big oxygen event.
Rodinia vs Pannotia: both are Proterozoic. Pannotia was short-lived and formed ~600 Ma; the supercontinent that comes later in the Paleozoic is Pangaea.

sections.title: Ice on a young Earth
bullets: Slide 24 (picture, no caption): two globes with a TIME arrow. Labels: sea ice, ice-covered land, mountains, equator. On the later globe, ice covers more of the planet. It is the picture for a Snowball-type glaciation (the term itself is not on the slide).

Textbook 15 (**Snowball Earth hypothesis**, controversial): around 700 Ma, ice spread from the poles toward the equator. Evidence: tropical limestone found interbedded with glacial deposits. A competing idea, **Slushball Earth**, keeps some equatorial ocean open.
Textbook 8.5: the first glaciation, the **Huron Glaciation** (about 2.1 Ga), followed the Great Oxygenation Event.
Slide 25: strata with **large clasts surrounded by mudstone**. The slide says glaciers can carry clasts of all sizes, so this mix points to glaciers.

boxes.text: Why did oxygen cause cooling? Free oxygen reacted with methane to make carbon dioxide. Methane traps heat better than carbon dioxide, so the greenhouse effect weakened and the planet cooled (Textbook 8.5).
Ice is a bad sorter: it dumps boulders and mud together. Rivers and waves sort by size (outside source, general knowledge).
The slides give no ages for slides 24 and 25. The 2.1 Ga and 700 Ma dates come from the textbook, and Snowball Earth is described there as controversial.

sections.title: Paleozoic geography: seas, orogens, terranes and Pangea
bullets: Slide 26 (~510 Ma, Cambrian-Ordovician): continents are scattered. **Gondwana** (South America, Africa, India, Antarctica, Australia) is one big mass; **Laurentia**, **Baltica** and **Siberia** are separate.

Slides 27-28: **Laurentia** (the North American craton) has dry land in the interior but a **shallow sea** and a **carbonate shelf** around it, a **transcontinental arch**, a **paleoequator** crossing it, plus labelled **passive margins** and **volcanic arcs** around the edges.
Textbook 8.6.1: sea level rose and fell four times in the Paleozoic. Each rise covered most of North America with a shallow tropical sea, recorded as limestone with fossil corals.

Slide 30 (Silurian-Devonian): oceans **Iapetus**, **Rheic**, **Paleotethys** and **Panthalassa** between Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia, Siberia and Kazakhstania. The **Caledonides** are the mountains where Laurentia meets Baltica. The **Taconic orogen** was a relict of an **Ordovician collision**.
Slide 31: **Antler orogen** (west), **Caledonian orogen**, **Acadian orogeny** and the **Catskill Delta** (east). A note says 'Terranes that eventually attach to Laurentia'.

**Terranes** are chunks of crust (such as island arcs and microcontinents) riding on a subducting plate that get stuck onto the edge of a continent (Textbook 2). Much of California is accreted terranes.
**Antler orogeny** (Devonian to Pennsylvanian): a volcanic island arc accreted onto western North America, subducting away from North America (Textbook 8.6.1).

Slides 35-36 (Carboniferous-Permian): the continents join into **Pangea**. Slide 36 labels the **Caledonian**, **Hercynian**, **Alleghanian** and **Ouachita** orogens, **Coal swamps** and the **Ancestral Rockies**.

Textbook 8.6.1: Pangea formed by island-arc accretion and continental collisions. In North America these were the **Taconic, Acadian, Caledonian and Alleghanian** orogenies. The Appalachians are their eroded remnants. The ocean around Pangea was **Panthalassa**. The **Tethys Sea** later split it into **Laurasia** and **Gondwana**.

boxes.text: Why did the mountains form on the east coast? When ocean basins close, the continents on either side collide and pile up mountains. Several such collisions closed the oceans between Laurentia, Baltica and Gondwana to make Pangea.
Panthalassa = 'all sea' and Pangea = 'all land'. Pan- means all.

Pannotia (Proterozoic, ~600 Ma) is not Pangea (late Paleozoic). Panthalassa is an ocean, Pangea is land. An orogen is the mountain belt; an orogeny is the event. In the late Paleozoic the east coast of North America had the high mountains and the west coast was smaller isolated volcanic highlands (Textbook 8.6.1).

sections.title: Paleozoic Era: life explodes, then nearly dies
bullets: Cambrian/Ordovician: shallow seas full of corals, trilobites, brachiopods, nautiloids (slide 29).
Silurian/Devonian: **vascular plants** spread (veins, woody tissue, seeds) and first forests appear. Then land animals (scorpions, spiders, insects) follow (slide 32).
End of Devonian: first **amphibians**. **Tiktaalik** (found 1996) is a lobe-finned fish with push-up fins and a neck (slide 33).
Permian extinction killed **90%** of marine species (slide 38).
Slide 34 is the Tiktaalik fossil (scale bar about 20 cm). Textbook 8.6.2 dates it about 385 Ma.

Slide 37 (picture only, no caption): a giant dragonfly next to a woman's silhouette for scale. Textbook 8.6.2: Carboniferous oxygen was the highest ever and gave the largest arthropods (the millipede Arthropleura was 2.5 m long). Linking the dragonfly to that is my inference.

Slide 38 graph (Fig. E.8) counts **genera** through time with the periods lettered along the bottom. The big drop at the end of the Permian (P) is the Permian extinction. The K/T mass extinction is also labelled.
Slide 39 (Abbott, Fig. 15.12) counts **families** of marine animals with hard skeletons. Five arrows mark mass extinctions. Textbook 8.6.2 says the end-Ordovician one was the earliest of five.

boxes.text: Why did animals follow plants onto land? Plants made food and shelter first, and insects ate them. Predators then followed the food.
Permian extinction number: slide says 90% of marine species; textbook says up to 96%. Use 90% from the slide.

The Permian extinction slide says 90% of marine SPECIES, but the graphs on slides 38 and 39 count genera and families. Do not mix the units. Textbook says up to 96% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrates.

sections.title: Mesozoic geography: Pangea splits and the west coast builds up
bullets: Slide 40 (Late Jurassic, ~150 Ma): Pangea has started splitting. A **mid-ocean ridge** opens between North America and Africa/South America, with trenches on other edges. Textbook 8.7.1: breakup began ~210 Ma in the Late Triassic. The Atlantic opened first in the middle, then the south, and last the north.

Slide 42 (Late Cretaceous, ~90 Ma) legend: **convergent boundary**, **thrust fault**, **volcanic arc**. Labels: **Trench**, **Sierran arc**, **Sevier fold-thrust belt**, **Western Interior Seaway**, **Coastal plain**. The inset cross-section shows an **accretionary prism**, then the Sierran arc, then the Sevier belt.
Slide 42 text: in the **early Cretaceous, several island arcs collided with western North America**.

Textbook 8.7.1: the **Cretaceous Interior Seaway** ran from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic and split North America into **Laramidia** (west) and **Appalachia** (east) for about 25 million years. Coal in Utah and Wyoming formed in swamps along its shores.

Slide 43 shows the **magnetic polarity time scale** (chrons Brunhes, Matuyama, Gauss, Gilbert, with named subchrons; black and white bands for the two polarities). Its caption says: 'The rate of convection in the outer core determines what kind of rocks are deposited on the continents in significant part.' The textbook does not discuss this claim. It only says magnetic reversals are the swapping of Earth's poles and are used for correlation (Textbook 2 and 7.4).

Slide 44 (Eocene map): red line = **eastern limit of Laramide**, yellow = **eastern limit of Sevier**, with the Canadian Rockies, Wyoming fold-thrust belt and US Rocky Mountains. Sevier (Cretaceous) was a thin-skinned fold-thrust belt. Laramide (early Cenozoic) was thick-skinned.

Slide 45 (70 Ma): the Atlantic is open with a **ridge axis** and **transform faults**; there are **subduction zones** along the west of the Americas and the north of the **Tethys Ocean**; India is south of the equator.
Slide 46: a Cretaceous world map. Light blue shows shallow seas flooding parts of the continents.

boxes.text: Why did a sea flood the middle of North America? Shallow subduction of a young, hot, light Farallon plate downwarped the interior. Sea level was also high from fast spreading, warmth and melted ice (Textbook 8.7.1).
Sevier = thin (shallow faults, 'S for stacks of slices'). Laramide = thick-skinned, deep rock, big Rockies bulges.

Slide 43 is odd: the picture is a magnetic reversal chart but the caption is about the outer core and rock types. Treat it as 'slide says so' and do not expect the textbook to explain it. Also the textbook puts the Laramide in the early Cenozoic even though the slide-44 map sits beside the Cretaceous slides.

sections.title: Mesozoic Era: age of dinosaurs
bullets: Cretaceous: modern fish, aquatic reptiles, giant turtles; **angiosperms** (flowering plants) spread (slide 47).
Dinosaurs lived in nearly every environment; pterosaurs flew; birds began to diversify; mammals got bigger brains (slide 48).
Slides 49-51: impact at ~66 Ma on the Yucatan peninsula (Earth at 66 Ma).

Slide 41 (picture): a Triassic-Jurassic scene with long-necked and plated dinosaurs and a flying pterosaur. Textbook 8.7.2: dinosaurs were small in the Triassic and became truly massive in the Jurassic; the end-Triassic extinction helped them and mammals rise. Mammals stayed small and mostly nocturnal.

boxes.text: Why did flowering plants spread fast? They make seeds quickly and use insects to carry pollen, so they reproduce faster than plants relying on wind.

sections.title: The K-Pg impact
bullets: Slide 49: artist's picture of the impact and a globe 'Earth at 66 Ma' with the strike location marked near the Gulf of Mexico. Slide 50: Google Earth view with the Yucatan Peninsula and a circle where the crater lies.

Slide 51 is a colour map of a ring-shaped structure at about 20 to 22 N, 89 to 90 W. The slide has no caption; it is presumably the geophysical map of the buried **Chicxulub crater**, so the ring is the crater.
Textbook 8.7: the extinction was likely caused by a large **bolide** that hit 66 Ma. 90% of plankton species, 75% of plant species and all the dinosaurs went extinct.

Evidence: **iridium** (rare on Earth, common in meteorites) in a worldwide layer at the K-T boundary, melted rock spheres, **shocked quartz**, a fern-rich layer after fires, and tsunami deposits from Texas to Alabama inferred as a 2 km tsunami.

**Chicxulub crater**: about 180 km wide, the third largest confirmed on Earth, confirmed in 1991 using petroleum-company geophysical data. Granite in the peak ring shows the impact lifted deep basement rock.
Other possible contributors: falling sea level and the **Deccan Traps** flood basalts in India (over 1.3 million km3).

boxes.text: Why was the crater hard to find? It is partly underwater and partly covered by dense forest on the Yucatan Peninsula, so it only showed up in geophysical data. An iridium layer worldwide points to a space rock because iridium is rare in Earth's crust.
Iridium = 'I came from space'.

K-T and K-Pg are the same boundary (Tertiary was renamed Paleogene). Date: slide 6 says 65 Ma, slide 49 and the textbook say 66 Ma. Birds descend from dinosaurs, so 'all the dinosaurs' means the non-bird dinosaurs.

sections.title: Cenozoic geography: moving continents, Basin and Range, ice ages
bullets: Slide 52: the world today with **arrows showing plate movement** and **present-day mountain belts** (Alpine-Himalayan, Cordilleran, Andean). The inset says **'The southern continents were moving north at 50 Ma.'**
Textbook 8.8.1: the **Tethys Sea** closed as Africa and India hit Eurasia, building the Alps, Zagros and Himalaya. The Himalaya collision began about 57 Ma and continues today.

Slide 53 (western US): **Sierra Nevada batholith**, **Basin and Range**, **Colorado Plateau**, **Rio Grande Rift**, **Snake River Plain**, **Yellowstone hot spot**, and arrows for the **opening direction**. The cross-section shows tilted fault blocks in the Basin and Range.

Textbook 8.8.1: the subduction zone consumed the ridge, so the west coast changed to a **transform boundary** (San Andreas). As it grew, east-west **extension** spread across the western US and made the **Basin and Range**.

Slide 56 (ice age): continental glacier, sea ice and unglaciated land. The **Bering Strait was a land bridge**, **New York City was under ice**, sea ice surrounded Iceland, and **large lakes formed in the Basin and Range Province**.

Slide 57: red lines show the **ice-age coastline**, far out from today's. Sea level fell **more than 100 m**, exposing shelves as land bridges for human and animal migrations. The Quaternary ice age began about 2.58 Ma (Textbook 8.8.2).

boxes.text: Why does the Alpine-Himalayan belt exist? Continents that were moving north ran into Eurasia, and collisions pile up mountains where the ocean between them closed.
Basin and Range = stretched pizza dough: pull the crust apart east-west and it breaks into tilted blocks (ranges) and drops (basins).
Laramide = squeezing and uplift (compression, thick-skinned). Basin and Range = stretching (extension). Both are in the western US but are opposite stresses.

sections.title: Cenozoic Era: age of mammals
bullets: After the **K-Pg boundary**, plants recovered; first grasses mid-Cenozoic; birds (dinosaur descendants) spread (slide 54).
Mammals diversified to fill empty niches (slide 55). Many giant mammals died off ~10 ka, possibly from human hunting.
Ice ages dropped sea level by more than **100 m**, exposing land bridges (slide 57).
Humans: primates ~20 Ma; human-like ~4 Ma; genus Homo 2.4 Ma; *H. erectus* ~1.6 Ma; *H. sapiens* ~500 ka; modern humans ~190 ka (slides 58-59).

boxes.text: Why did land bridges appear? Ice sheets locked up ocean water, so sea level fell and shallow shelves became dry land.

sections.title: End-of-deck clicker questions
bullets: Slide 60: 'The iron in the steel in my car was probably deposited during an ______?' Answer **D, ocean oxygenation event**. Banded iron formations formed when oxygen rusted iron out of seawater (slide 21).
Slide 61: 'The continental crust was mostly extracted from the mantle during the ______?' Answer **B, Archean** (slide 10 curve: about 80% by 2.5 Ga).

Slide 62: 'The continental crust may have been mostly extracted from the mantle by ______?' Best answer **C, subduction zones**. The slide shows no answer, but slides 7 and 9 build continents from volcanic arcs.

boxes.text: These three questions summarize the lecture: oxygen gave us iron ore, the Archean made the crust, and subduction was the likely machine.
Slide 62 says 'may have been', so it is a hypothesis. Hot spots make oceanic plateaus and greenstone, not most of the continental crust.

quiz.q: The iron in the steel in a car was probably deposited during a(n) ______?
quiz.why: Dissolved iron rusted out of the ocean when oxygen appeared, forming banded iron formations, the main source of iron ore.

quiz.q: The continental crust was mostly extracted from the mantle during the ______?
quiz.why: The slide 10 graph shows about 80% of present continental area already existed by the end of the Archean.

quiz.q: The continental crust may have been mostly extracted from the mantle by ______?
quiz.why: Water-rich subduction melts mantle rock into felsic magma, which builds island arcs that merge into continents (slides 7 and 9). Confirm this with your prof: slide 62 does not give the answer.

quiz.q:
Which statements about the Hadean Eon are correct?
I. It began with planetesimal accretion.
II. Iron sank to form the core.
III. Banded iron formations formed then.
quiz.why: I and II are on slide 3. BIFs need oxygen, which came in the Proterozoic, so III is wrong.

quiz.q: Banded iron formations are evidence for:
quiz.why: Slide 21 says it directly: BIFs preserve evidence of oxygen build-up.

quiz.q: Pannotia was a supercontinent that:
options: lasted for over a billion years
formed about 600 Ma and broke apart soon after
quiz.why: Slide 20: Pannotia was short-lived, forming ~600 Ma at the end of the Proterozoic.

quiz.q: Tiktaalik is important because it:
options: is a fossil transitional between fish and amphibians
quiz.why: It was a lobe-finned fish that could do push-ups and look around on a swivel-jointed neck, a mix of fish and land traits.

quiz.q:
Which statements about the Cenozoic are correct?
I. It is known as the Age of Mammals.
II. Glacial advances lowered sea level by more than 100 m.
III. Birds are descendants of dinosaurs.
quiz.why: All three are on slides 54, 55 and 57.

quiz.q: Reasoning: Land bridges between continents appeared during glacial advances because:
options: ice locked up water so sea level fell
quiz.why: Water trapped as ice lowers sea level, exposing shallow continental shelves as dry land.

quiz.q: The Permian extinction eradicated about what share of marine species?
quiz.why: Slide says 90%. (Note: the textbook says up to 96%; use the slide's value.)

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT labelled on the slide 7 cross-section?
quiz.why: Slide 7 labels volcanic arcs, an oceanic plateau, a rift, lithospheric mantle, oceanic crust, magma and sediment, but no mid-ocean ridge.

quiz.q: Reasoning: On slide 18 the crust of North America gets younger moving out from the Archean core. What does this tell you about how the continent grew?
options: It formed all at once from a single magma ocean at 4.5 Ga.
It grew by repeated meteorite impacts in its centre.
It grew by adding younger crust around an older Archean core.
Sea-floor spreading split the Archean core apart.
quiz.why: The legend shows Archean provinces (>2.5 Ga) in the middle and belts of 2.0 to 1.0 Ga added toward the edge, so the continent grew outward by accretion.

quiz.q:
Which statements about a craton are correct?
I. It has a shield and a platform.
II. The shield is crystalline basement rock near the surface.
III. The platform is sedimentary rock covering the shield.
quiz.why: All three are in Textbook 8.4.2 and match the Shield and platform labels on slide 17.

quiz.q: Slide 25 shows strata with large clasts surrounded by mudstone. This suggests deposition by:
options: a quiet deep ocean with no currents
glaciers, which carry clasts of all sizes
quiz.why: The slide caption says glaciers can carry clasts of all sizes, so big clasts in fine mud point to glaciers.

quiz.q: Which statement about Paleozoic geography is INCORRECT?
options: The Antler orogeny accreted a volcanic island arc onto the east coast of North America.
The Taconic orogen was a relict of an Ordovician collision.
Shallow seas repeatedly covered much of North America.
Pangea was assembled by the late Paleozoic.
Coal swamps existed in the Carboniferous.
quiz.why: The Antler orogeny was on the west coast. The east coast had the Taconic, Acadian, Caledonian and Alleghanian orogenies.

quiz.q: Reasoning: Marine limestone with fossil corals is found in the middle of North America. This most likely records:
options: a rise in sea level that flooded the continent with a shallow tropical sea
quiz.why: Textbook 8.6.1 ties Paleozoic sea-level rises to shallow tropical seas over North America, recorded as limestone with fossil corals.

quiz.q:
Which statements are correct?
I. Pangea was completed by the late Paleozoic.
II. The Tethys Sea eventually divided Pangea into Laurasia and Gondwana.
III. Pangea was surrounded by the Tethys Ocean.
quiz.why: I and II are in Textbook 8.6.1. Pangea was surrounded by Panthalassa, while the Tethys was a bay cut into it, so III is wrong.

quiz.q: Slide 42 shows a trench, the Sierran arc and the Sevier fold-thrust belt. What does this tell you about the western margin of North America in the Cretaceous?
options: a passive margin with no volcanism
a transform boundary like the San Andreas
a rift opening a new ocean
quiz.why: A trench with a volcanic arc and a thrust belt is a subduction setting, and the slide legend marks the boundary as convergent.

quiz.q: Reasoning: Why did a shallow sea (the Western Interior Seaway) flood the middle of North America in the Cretaceous?
options: Sea level was high and shallow subduction of the Farallon plate downwarped the interior.
A giant impact dug a basin.
Glaciers melted at the end of the Cenozoic ice age.
quiz.why: Textbook 8.7.1 says shallow subduction downwarped central North America and high sea levels let the sea flood it.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT evidence linking the K-Pg extinction to an impact?
options: banded iron formations laid down at the boundary
a crater about 180 km wide on the Yucatan Peninsula
quiz.why: Banded iron formations record ocean oxygenation in the Proterozoic. The other four are impact evidence in Textbook 8.7.

quiz.q: Reasoning: Why was the Chicxulub crater hard to find?
options: It is only about 18 m wide.
It is partly underwater and hidden under dense forest, so geophysical data were needed.
quiz.why: Textbook 8.7: the crater is about 180 km wide but partly underwater and obscured by forest, so it was confirmed in 1991 using petroleum-company geophysical data.

quiz.q:
Which statements about Cenozoic geography are correct?
I. At 50 Ma the southern continents were moving north.
II. Closing the Tethys Sea built mountain belts such as the Alps and Himalaya.
III. The Himalaya collision began about 57 Ma and continues today.
quiz.why: I is the slide 52 inset. II and III are in Textbook 8.8.1.

quiz.q: Reasoning: The Basin and Range province of the western US formed mainly because:
options: east-west stretching spread across the west after the subduction zone became the San Andreas transform
a large impact stretched the crust
quiz.why: Textbook 8.8.1: as the San Andreas grew, east-west extension spread over the western US and made the Basin and Range. Laramide was compression, not stretching.

cards.back: Earth's first eon, 4.57 to 3.8 Ga. It begins when Earth forms by planetesimal accretion.
Small bodies (planetesimals) collide and stick together to build up a planet.
cards.short: Small bodies stick together to build Earth

cards.back: In molten Earth, gravity pulled iron to the centre. The ultramafic mantle stayed as a thick outer shell.
cards.short: Iron sinks to the core; mantle stays outside

cards.back: Gravitational collapse, impacts, and radioactive decay.
The eon after the Hadean, ending 2.5 Ga. Most of today's continental area grew during it (about 80% by the end).
A layered mound made by microbial mats. Earliest well-preserved fossils, ~3.5 Ga.
cards.short: Layered mound built by microbial mats

cards.back: protero = first, zoic = life. Runs 2.5 Ga to 542 Ma (slide 6).
Layers of iron oxide and silica that preserve evidence of oxygen build-up in the oceans.
A Proterozoic supercontinent, shown at about 750 Ma.
A short-lived supercontinent that formed about 600 Ma and broke apart soon after.
Soft-bodied, multicellular invertebrates resembling worms and jellyfish, at the end of the Proterozoic.
The eon from 542 Ma to today. Name means 'visible life'. (Textbook says 541 Ma.)
Plants with internal veins to move water, woody tissue, and seeds. They formed the first forests (Silurian-Devonian).
cards.short: Plants with veins, wood and seeds

cards.back: A lobe-finned fish with push-up fins and a swivel neck, found in 1996. Transitional between fish and amphibians.
Ended the Paleozoic and wiped out 90% of marine species. (Textbook says up to 96%.)
Flowering plants. They make seeds quickly and use insects for pollination. Spread in the Cretaceous.
Marks the end-Cretaceous mass extinction ~66 Ma, linked to an impact on the Yucatan peninsula (Chicxulub).
Known as the Age of Mammals. Mammals diversified to fill niches left empty after the K-Pg extinction.
Dropped more than 100 m because water was trapped as ice, creating land bridges.
The first members of the human genus appeared about 2.4 Ma.
Appeared ~1.6 Ma and could make stone axes.
Appeared ~500 ka. Modern humans appeared ~190 ka.
The stable interior of a continent, mostly formed in the Archean. It has a shield (crystalline basement) and a platform (sedimentary cover).
One thousand, one million, and one billion years ago.
Modern fish, aquatic reptiles, giant turtles, flowering plants, dinosaurs in nearly every environment, soaring pterosaurs, diversifying birds, and mammals with bigger brains.
A belt of dark metamorphosed volcanic rock (greenstone = metamorphosed basalt) squeezed between arcs and plateaus as an early continent assembled.
cards.short: Squeezed dark volcanic rock in early continents

cards.back: A chain of volcanoes formed where an oceanic plate subducts under another oceanic plate. Several arcs can combine into a continent.
cards.short: Volcano chain above subduction; builds continents

cards.back: Shield = crystalline basement rock at the surface. Platform = sedimentary rock covering the shield. Both are parts of a craton.
An Archean core (>2.5 Ga) was ringed by younger belts: 2.0-1.8 Ga, Yavapai 1.8-1.7, Mazatzal 1.7-1.6, granite-rhyolite 1.5-1.3, and Grenville 1.3-1.0 Ga at the edge.
cards.short: Old core, younger belts added outward

cards.back: Strata with big clasts surrounded by mudstone point to glaciers, which can carry clasts of all sizes.
cards.short: Glacier deposit: all clast sizes mixed

cards.back: A mountain belt on the east of Laurentia, a relict of an Ordovician collision.
A volcanic island arc accreted onto western North America, Devonian to Pennsylvanian, subducting away from North America.
cards.short: Island arc added to western North America

cards.back: Pieces of crust, such as island arcs, that later attach to a continent, as in 'Terranes that eventually attach to Laurentia'.
cards.short: Crust chunks that later stick to a continent

cards.back: All major continents grouped as one by the late Paleozoic, ringed by Panthalassa. The Tethys Sea later split it into Laurasia and Gondwana.
Huge forests and swamps of the Carboniferous became the coal that powered the Industrial Revolution (labelled on slide 36).
A Cretaceous shallow sea from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic. It split North America into Laramidia and Appalachia.
The K-Pg impact crater under the Yucatan Peninsula, about 180 km wide, confirmed in 1991 with geophysical data.
A rare-on-Earth element found worldwide in the K-T boundary layer. It is more common in meteorites, so it is evidence of an impact.
cards.short: Rare element at K-T boundary: impact clue

cards.back: A western US province stretched east-west after the San Andreas transform grew, making tilted fault blocks.
They were moving north toward Eurasia, closing the Tethys Sea and building the Alps and Himalaya.

eons.name: Hadean
eons.note: Molten start. Earth forms, heats up, and the iron core separates. Dates are from slide 6 (textbook: 4.5 to 4.0 Ga).

eons.name: Archean
eons.note: First continents and microbial life. By the end, about 80% of today's continental area existed.

eons.name: Proterozoic
eons.note: Oxygen builds up, supercontinents form and break, and the first complex animals appear at the very end.

eons.name: Phanerozoic
eons.note: 'Visible life'. The time of shells, bones, forests, dinosaurs, mammals and humans. Tap an era in the bottom bar to zoom.

eras.name: Paleozoic
eras.note: Old life. Shells, fish, land plants, first land animals; ends with the Permian extinction. (Textbook: ends 252 Ma.)

eras.name: Mesozoic
eras.note: Middle life. Age of dinosaurs. Ends at the K-Pg boundary (slide 6 says 65 Ma; slide 49 and the textbook say 66 Ma).

eras.name: Cenozoic
eras.note: Recent life. Age of Mammals, ice ages and the rise of humans.

events.title: Earth forms
events.text: Earth forms by planetesimal accretion, then heats up from gravitational collapse, impacts and radioactive decay.
events.why: Collisions and compression release heat, and radioactive atoms keep releasing it.

events.title: Earth partly melts
events.text: Hot enough to partially melt by ~4.5 Ga. Molten iron sinks to form the core; the ultramafic mantle stays as a thick shell.
events.why: Iron is denser than rock, so gravity sorts it to the centre.

events.title: Stromatolites
events.text: Layered microbial mats leave the first well-preserved fossils.

events.title: Archean ends: continents mostly grown
events.text: About 80% of today's continental area existed by this time.

events.title: Banded iron formations
events.text: Iron oxide layers record oxygen building up in the oceans.
events.why: Dissolved iron rusts out of seawater when oxygen appears. No oxygen, no rust bands.

events.title: Rodinia assembles
events.text: Continents collide to form a supercontinent. Slide 19 shows it at about 750 Ma.

events.title: Rodinia breaks up
events.text: Breakup runs from about 750 to 600 Ma, making shallow seas where life could evolve.

events.title: Pannotia
events.text: A short-lived supercontinent that formed about 600 Ma and broke apart soon after.

events.title: Ediacara fauna
events.text: Soft-bodied, multicellular invertebrates resembling worms and jellyfish appear at the end of the Proterozoic.
events.why: Bodies without shells rarely fossilise, which is why Precambrian fossils are rare (Textbook 8.6).

events.title: Cambrian and Ordovician seas
events.text: Corals, trilobites, brachiopods and nautiloids fill shallow seas.

events.title: End-Ordovician extinction
events.text: An ice age lowered sea level; the earliest of five mass extinctions in the fossil record.

events.title: First forests and land animals
events.text: Vascular plants (veins, wood, seeds) spread and form the first forests. Scorpions, spiders, insects and crustaceans follow onto land.
events.why: Plants came first, so animals had food and shelter on land.

events.title: Tiktaalik
events.text: A lobe-finned fish with push-up fins and a swivel neck, transitional between fish and amphibians (found 1996). The first amphibians appear at the end of the Devonian.

events.title: Pangaea assembles
events.text: All major continents are grouped together by the late Paleozoic.

events.title: Permian extinction
events.text: Ends the Paleozoic. Wipes out 90% of marine species (textbook: up to 96%).
events.why: Leading idea (textbook): huge Siberian Traps volcanism added greenhouse gases that disrupted climate and food chains.

events.title: End-Triassic extinction
events.text: The fourth of the major mass extinctions. It helped mammals and dinosaurs rise.

events.title: Cretaceous world
events.text: Flowering plants spread, dinosaurs live everywhere, pterosaurs fly, birds diversify, mammals get larger brains.
events.why: Flowers make seeds fast and use insects for pollination.

events.title: K-Pg impact and extinction
events.text: An impact on the Yucatan peninsula (Chicxulub crater) coincides with the extinction of the dinosaurs.

events.title: Grasses appear
events.text: First grasses in the middle Cenozoic. Plant life recovered after K-Pg and birds spread.

events.title: Ape-like primates diversify
events.text: Miocene.

events.title: First human-like primate
events.text: Appears about 4 Ma.

events.title: Quaternary ice ages
events.text: Glacial advances lock up water as ice; sea level falls more than 100 m, exposing land bridges.
events.why: Ice sheets hold ocean water, so shelves dry out.

events.title: Genus Homo
events.text: First members of the human genus.

events.title: Homo erectus
events.text: Could make stone axes.

events.title: Homo sapiens
events.text: Appears ~500 ka.

events.title: Modern humans
events.text: Appear ~190 ka.

events.title: Giant mammals die off
events.text: Mammoths, mastodons and ground sloths died off ~10 ka, possibly because of hunting by humans.
